title: Imbolc, St Brigid's Day and Candlemas
when_text: 1 February, St Brigid's Day and the Gaelic start of spring; Candlemas follows on 2 February
intro: Imbolc, halfway between the winter solstice and the spring equinox, was one of the four Gaelic seasonal festivals and became the feast of St Brigid of Kildare. Its customs, from rush crosses to beds made for the saint and visits to holy wells, were kept in Ireland, Gaelic Scotland and the Isle of Man, and since 2023 the day has been a public holiday in Ireland. Next day comes Candlemas, the old end of the Christmas season.

facts.title: A tomb that faces the Imbolc sunrise
facts.text: The passage of the Mound of the Hostages on the Hill of Tara, built between about 3350 and 2800 BC, faces the sunrise around Imbolc and Samhain, at the start of February and November. Some see this as a sign that the date mattered in the Neolithic; the archaeoastronomer Frank Prendergast thinks such alignments are so rare they are probably chance.

sources.title: Mound of the Hostages (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: At this mound, the passage is illuminated on the mornings of Samhain and Imbolc, at the beginning of November and February, respectively.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Frank Prendergast argues that this alignment is so rare that it is a product of chance.

facts.title: When the ewes are milked
facts.text: Imbolc is named as one of the four seasonal festivals in the tale Tochmarc Emire, which survives in a tenth-century version, as the time 'when the ewes are milked at spring's beginning'. The meaning of the word itself is uncertain; 'in the belly', for the pregnant ewes, is one common explanation.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The tale Tochmarc Emire, which survives in a 10th-century version, names Imbolc as one of four seasonal festivals, and says it is "when the ewes are milked at spring's beginning".

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The etymology of Imbolc or Imbolg is unclear.

facts.title: Brigid of Kildare
facts.text: Brigid, who is said to have lived from about 451 to 525, is with Patrick and Columba one of Ireland's three national saints. Her Lives say she founded the abbey of Kildare, but there is little firm evidence about her, and some historians think the saint took on features of the goddess Brigid. Tradition places her birth at Faughart in County Louth.

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: is the patroness saint (or 'mother saint') of Ireland, and one of its three national saints along with Patrick and Columba

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There is little historical evidence of her.

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Some historians suggest that Brigid is a Christianisation of the Celtic goddess Brigid.

facts.title: The fire nineteen nuns kept
facts.text: In the late twelfth century Gerald of Wales wrote that nineteen nuns at Kildare took turns to keep a fire burning in Brigid's honour, a fire said to have burned since her own time, inside a hedge no man could cross.

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the late 12th century, Gerald of Wales wrote that nineteen nuns took turns keeping a perpetual fire burning at Kildare in honour of Brigid, and that this fire had been burning since Brigid's time. He said it was ringed by a hedge that no man was allowed to cross.

facts.title: Brigid's crosses
facts.text: On St Brigid's Day people weave crosses of rushes, often with a diamond at the centre, and hang them over doors, windows and byres against fire, lightning and illness until the next year. The cross was part of RTÉ's logo from 1962 to 1995.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: They are traditionally hung over doors, windows, and stables to welcome Brigid and for protection against fire, lightning, illness, and evil spirits.

sources.title: Brigid's cross (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: From 1962 to 1995, it was incorporated into the Raidió Teilifís Éireann logo.

facts.title: A bed for Brigid
facts.text: On St Brigid's Eve families made a bed for the saint and left out food, drink and clothes for her to bless. In the Hebrides, where the custom is recorded from the seventeenth century, a doll called the dealbh Bríde was laid in a bed of hay and she was called in three times; in Ireland girls carried a Brigid doll, the Brídeóg, round the houses.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The custom of making Brigid's bed was prevalent in the Hebrides of Scotland, where it was recorded as far back as the 17th century.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: People also made a doll of Brigid (a Brídeóg), which was paraded around the community by girls

facts.title: Laa'l Breeshey on Man
facts.text: In the eighteenth-century Isle of Man people stood at the door with a bundle of rushes and invited the saint in: 'Brede, Brede, come to my house tonight.' The island's northern parish of Bride is named after her; its old church, demolished in 1870, went back to the thirteenth century.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 18th-century Mann, the custom was to stand at the door with a bundle of rushes and say "Brede, Brede, come to my house tonight. Open the door for Brede and let Brede come in".

sources.title: Bride, Isle of Man (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The previous parish church, a "simple structure" 30 yards east of the current church and demolished in 1870, dated back to the 13th century.

facts.title: Hoping for bad weather
facts.text: Gaelic lore says the Cailleach, the old hag of winter, gathers her firewood at Imbolc. If she wants winter to last she makes the day bright so she can collect plenty, so a wet, foul Imbolc was good news. On Man she was said to fly about as a huge bird carrying sticks in her beak.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: people would be relieved if Imbolc is a day of foul weather, as it means the Cailleach is asleep and winter is almost over

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the Cailleach is said to take the form of a gigantic bird carrying sticks in her beak

facts.title: Rounds at Brigid's wells
facts.text: Holy wells are visited on St Brigid's Day, with prayers said while walking sunwise round the well and coins or rags left behind. At St Brigid's Well near Liscannor in County Clare the rounds climb steps to a carved cross, which is circled and kissed, and come back down to the well.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: People traditionally visit holy wells and pray for health while walking 'sunwise' around the well.

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: St Brigid’s Well in Liscannor has a rosary-shaped path for visitors to walk as they pray

facts.title: Three saints in one grave
facts.text: Around 878, it is said, Brigid's relics were taken from Kildare to Downpatrick for fear of the Vikings and laid in the tomb of Patrick and Columba. John de Courcy reported finding all three in 1185 and reburied them in Down Cathedral the next year; a head said to be hers is kept near Lisbon.

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: About the year 878, owing to Viking raids, Brigid's relics were purportedly taken to Downpatrick and reburied in the tomb of St Patrick and St Columba.

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The relics of the three saints were said to have been found in 1185 by John de Courcy, and on 9 June of the following year he had them solemnly reburied in Down Cathedral.

facts.title: A London church and the wedding cake
facts.text: St Bride's in Fleet Street is named after Brigid and may have been founded by Irish missionaries; it is at least the seventh church on its site. Its tiered Wren spire is said to have inspired a baker's apprentice from Ludgate Hill to make the first tiered wedding cake in 1703.

sources.title: St Bride's Church (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is believed that its name is derived from Bridget of Ireland, the patron saint of Ireland. It may have been founded by Irish monks

sources.title: St Bride's Church (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Traditional wedding cakes are said to date back to 1703 when Thomas Rich, a baker's apprentice from Ludgate Hill wanted to make an extravagant cake, and drew on the design of St Bride's Church for inspiration.

facts.title: Candlemas ends Christmas
facts.text: Candlemas on 2 February, the feast of the Presentation of Christ in the Temple, is one of the church's oldest feasts. In medieval and Tudor England it, rather than Twelfth Night, marked the end of the Christmas season, and in Scotland it was one of the four quarter days on which rents fell due.

sources.title: Twelfth Night (holiday) (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In medieval and Tudor England, Candlemas traditionally marked the end of the Christmas season

sources.title: Scottish term days (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Term Days are Whitsunday and Martinmas, and together with Candlemas and Lammas they constitute the Quarter Days.

sources.title: Candlemas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Feast of the Presentation or Purification is one of the oldest feasts of the church.

facts.title: A new public holiday
facts.text: Since 2023 'Imbolc/St Brigid's Day' has been a public holiday in Ireland.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Since 2023, "Imbolc/St Brigid's Day" has been an annual public holiday in Ireland.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)

places.why: Passage tomb cemetery on Slieve na Calliagh; its Cairn L is also aligned with the sunrise around Imbolc and Samhain.

sources.title: Imbolc (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A few passage tombs in Ireland are aligned with the sunrise around the times of Imbolc and Samhain.

places.name: Kildare Cathedral
places.why: Thirteenth-century cathedral on the site of the abbey said to have been founded by Brigid, where her fire was kept.

sources.title: Kildare Cathedral (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: it was built in the 13th century on the site of an important Celtic Christian abbey, which is said to have been founded by Saint Brigid in the 5th century

places.name: Kildare Round Tower
places.why: Round tower in the grounds of St Brigid's Cathedral, Kildare.

sources.title: Kildare Cathedral (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There is an Irish round tower in the cathedral grounds.

places.name: Faughart
places.why: Hill near Dundalk held by tradition to be Brigid's birthplace, with church ruins, a medieval graveyard, holy wells and a shrine to her.

sources.title: Faughart (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Hill of Faughart is the site of early Christian church ruins and a medieval graveyard, as well as a shrine to Saint Brigid. According to tradition, it was the birthplace of Saint Brigid of Kildare in 451 AD.

places.name: St Brigid's Well, Faughart
places.why: One of the holy wells at Faughart visited by pilgrims to Brigid's shrine.

sources.title: Faughart (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There are also two holy wells and a modern shrine devoted to Saint Brigid, which attracts thousands of pilgrims and tourists each year.

places.name: St Brigid's Well, Liscannor
places.why: Holy well near the Cliffs of Moher with a path of rounds up to a carved cross.

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: ascending steps to a carved sandstone cross which must be circled, touched, and kissed five times before descending the pathway back to the well shrine

places.name: Down Cathedral
places.why: Where the relics of Brigid, Patrick and Columba are said to have been reburied in 1186.

sources.title: Brigid of Kildare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: he had them solemnly reburied in Down Cathedral

places.name: St Bride's Church, Fleet Street
places.why: Ancient London church named after Brigid, perhaps founded by Irish missionaries.

sources.title: St Bride's Church (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Likely dedicated to Saint Bridget perhaps as early as the 6th century
